newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: More than 25 said dead in Cambodia custody.
newsitem.headline: More than 25 said dead in Cambodia custody.

text.p: More than 25 supporters of Cambodia's royalist party have died in custody since the July 6 ouster of First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, a Western source in diplomatic circles said on Monday.
The source, who declined to be identified, said there was also evidence that some of the detainees picked up in the aftermath of two days of fighting in the capital on July 5 and 6 had been tortured.
"More than 25 persons have died in government custody (since Ranariddh's ouster). These are soldiers, police and other opposition figures," the source said.
"You can use that number with confidence," he said.
Ranariddh was ousted by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen after fighting in the capital between forces loyal to the rival premiers.
Hun Sen said he had to take action against Ranariddh's men because the prince's military commanders were smuggling defectors from the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group into the city.

Foreign sources said on Sunday that hundreds of soldiers and supporters of Ranariddh had been detained and political killings and other abuses which occurred in the aftermath of Hun Sen's bloody overthrow of Ranariddh were continuing.

Government officals under Hun Sen said a senior official in Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party, Ho Sok, a secretary of state at the interior ministry, was picked up by soldiers on July 7 and later shot dead by "angry armed men".
On Monday, Hun Sen said another senior royalist, Chao Sambath, a FUNCINPEC intelligence officer, was killed in the fighting.
Hun Sen also said on Monday that human rights groups could check on the rights situation in the country.
"Human rights organisations, both local and outside, can check on the situation," he told reporters while on a trip to Kompong Thom province, north of the capital.
London-based human rights group Amnesty International said at the weekend it had grave fears for the safety of the detainees picked up after Ranariddh's ouster.
The Western official said on Monday that witnesses had spoken of the torture of some detainees.
"There is systematic torture and this information is substantiated by eye-witness accounts," he said.
He said his information was based on a brief and far from exhaustive investigation.
Foreign sources, speaking on condition they were not identified, said on Sunday that some embassies had refused asylum to Ranariddh's supporters, despite several political killings.
The sources said that the U.S. and Australian embassies were among the missions which had been refusing to protect fearful supporters of Ranariddh.
But Australia's ambassador in Phnom Penh denied that his embassy had refused asylum to frightened opponents of co-premier Hun Sen in the aftermath of the violent ouster of his coalition partner.
"It's not true," ambassador Tony Kevin told Reuters. "No one asked for asylum in our compound." A U.S. embassy official said opponents of Hun Sen were not categorically being turned away.
